intro: Four literary ways to say "the instant X happened, Y happened". Except for そばから, which also takes the た-form, each attaches to the dictionary form of a verb, and the second half reports something that really happened, never a plan, a wish or a request. They differ in what they stress: や否や is the neutral written form, が早いか stresses how fast the reaction was, なり describes a sudden, surprising action by the same person, and そばから says a result is undone each time, over and over.

skills.rule: Dictionary-form verb + や否や (or just や), then a past event: "the moment X happened, Y happened".
skills.explain:
や否や literally means "whether or not": X had hardly happened when Y followed. It is written or formal-narrative Japanese; in conversation people say たとたん or とすぐ. The short form や (聞くや) is even more literary.

The verb before it is always the dictionary form, even when the story is in the past: 開けるや否や, never 開けたや否や. The tense of the whole sentence comes from the second half, which is almost always past.

The two halves may have the same subject or different ones (ベルが鳴るや否や、学生たちが出ていった). The second half is often a reaction or an unexpected event.

It cannot introduce anything not yet real: no ～てください, ～よう, ～つもり or ～たい after it. For "as soon as you arrive, call me" use 着いたらすぐ.

examples.jp: ドアを開[あ]ける{や否[いな]や}、猫[ねこ]が飛[と]び出[だ]してきた。
examples.en: The moment I opened the door, the cat shot out.

examples.jp: ベルが鳴[な]る{や否[いな]や}、学生[がくせい]たちは教室[きょうしつ]を出[で]ていった。
examples.en: The instant the bell rang, the students left the classroom.

examples.jp: 彼[かれ]は駅[えき]に着[つ]く{や否[いな]や}、母親[ははおや]に電話[でんわ]をかけた。
examples.en: As soon as he reached the station, he phoned his mother.

examples.jp: 新製品[しんせいひん]は発売[はつばい]される{や否[いな]や}、売[う]り切[き]れてしまった。
examples.en: The new product sold out the moment it went on sale.

examples.jp: その知[し]らせを聞[き]く{や}、彼女[かのじょ]は家[いえ]を飛[と]び出[だ]した。
examples.en: The moment she heard the news, she rushed out of the house.

contrast.note: たとたん(に) is the everyday spoken equivalent and takes the た-form (立ち上がったとたん). や否や takes the dictionary form and belongs to writing.
Same structure and meaning, but が早いか paints the reaction as almost too quick, usually a hasty action by the subject. や否や is the neutral literary choice.
なり needs the same subject in both halves and a surprising action by that person. や否や allows a different subject (the bell rang, the students left).

mistakes.bad: 家[いえ]に帰[かえ]った{や否[いな]や}、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]り出[だ]した。
mistakes.good: 家[いえ]に帰[かえ]る{や否[いな]や}、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]り出[だ]した。
mistakes.note: The verb before や否や stays in the dictionary form; the past tense goes at the end.

mistakes.bad: 駅[えき]に着[つ]く{や否[いな]や}、電話[でんわ]してください。
mistakes.good: 駅[えき]に着[つ]い{たら}すぐ、電話[でんわ]してください。
mistakes.note: や否や reports past events; it cannot lead into a request. Use たらすぐ.

skills.tip: Read it as "had barely X-ed when": if the English is a story about the past, や否や fits; if it is an instruction or a plan, it does not.

skills.rule: Dictionary-form verb + が早いか, then a past action: "no sooner had X happened than Y", stressing the speed.
skills.explain:
が早いか literally asks "was it X that came first?": the two events were so close that you can hardly tell which came first. It is literary and vivid, typical of narrative writing.

The verb before it is normally the dictionary form (終わるが早いか); the た-form is occasionally seen in writing but is not needed. The second half is past and is usually a quick, often hasty action: ran out, fell asleep, spent it all, fled.

Like や否や, it describes events that actually happened. It cannot lead into a request, an invitation or a plan; for those use たらすぐ.

The subjects of the two halves can be the same (he got into bed and was asleep) or different (the shop opened and customers poured in).

examples.jp: 弟[おとうと]は布団[ふとん]に入[はい]る{が早[はや]いか}、眠[ねむ]ってしまった。
examples.en: No sooner had my little brother got into bed than he fell asleep.

examples.jp: 子供[こども]たちは授業[じゅぎょう]が終[お]わる{が早[はや]いか}、校庭[こうてい]へ走[はし]っていった。
examples.en: The minute class was over, the children ran off to the playground.

examples.jp: 店[みせ]が開[ひら]く{が早[はや]いか}、客[きゃく]が一斉[いっせい]に入[はい]ってきた。
examples.en: No sooner had the shop opened than customers poured in all at once.

examples.jp: 犯人[はんにん]は警官[けいかん]の姿[すがた]を見[み]る{が早[はや]いか}、逃[に]げ出[だ]した。
examples.en: The criminal took off the instant he caught sight of the police officer.

examples.jp: 兄[あに]は給料[きゅうりょう]を受[う]け取[と]る{が早[はや]いか}、全部[ぜんぶ]使[つか]ってしまった。
examples.en: No sooner had my brother been paid than he spent the lot.

contrast.note: や否や is the neutral literary "the moment". が早いか adds the picture of someone reacting almost before the first event is over.
そばから is for something that happens again and again and undoes the effort. が早いか describes one quick reaction.
たとたん is spoken and often an unexpected, uncontrolled event (めまいがした). が早いか is written and usually a deliberate, hasty action.

mistakes.bad: 家[いえ]に着[つ]く{が早[はや]いか}、連絡[れんらく]しよう。
mistakes.good: 家[いえ]に着[つ]い{たら}すぐ連絡[れんらく]しよう。
mistakes.note: が早いか cannot lead into a plan or intention (～よう).

mistakes.bad: 席[せき]に着[つ]く{が早[はや]いか}、教科書[きょうかしょ]を開[ひら]きなさい。
mistakes.good: 席[せき]に着[つ]い{たら}すぐ、教科書[きょうかしょ]を開[ひら]きなさい。
mistakes.note: No commands after が早いか; it narrates what already happened.

skills.tip: Picture a sprinter off the blocks: が早いか is for someone who reacted almost before X was over.

skills.rule: Dictionary-form verb + なり, same person in both halves: "as soon as he did X, he suddenly did Y".
skills.explain:
なり links two actions by one person with no gap, and the second is sudden or surprising to the observer: he walked in and burst out crying, she saw me and turned away. It is written or formal-narrative style.

Three conditions hold. The subject is the same in both halves. The subject is normally someone other than the speaker, because it reports what you saw someone do. The second half is a past event, never a request, intention or plan.

Do not mix it up with two other なり: Vたなり means "and stayed that way" (出ていったなり戻らない, he left and never came back), and NなりNなり means "either N or N" (電話なりメールなり).

For an event with a different subject (he came in and the phone rang) use や否や or たとたん.
patterns: [person] は [dictionary-form verb] なり、[sudden past action of the same person]

examples.jp: 父[ちち]は家[いえ]に帰[かえ]る{なり}、ソファーに倒[たお]れ込[こ]んだ。
examples.en: The moment my father got home, he collapsed onto the sofa.

examples.jp: 彼女[かのじょ]は私[わたし]の顔[かお]を見[み]る{なり}、泣[な]き出[だ]した。
examples.en: She burst into tears the moment she saw my face.

examples.jp: 兄[あに]は部屋[へや]に入[はい]る{なり}、窓[まど]を全部[ぜんぶ]開[あ]けた。
examples.en: As soon as my brother entered the room, he threw open all the windows.

examples.jp: 客[きゃく]は料理[りょうり]を一口[ひとくち]食[た]べる{なり}、顔[かお]をしかめた。
examples.en: The customer grimaced the moment he took a bite of the food.

examples.jp: 部長[ぶちょう]は報告書[ほうこくしょ]を読[よ]む{なり}、黙[だま]って席[せき]を立[た]った。
examples.en: As soon as the manager read the report, he got up from his seat without a word.

contrast.note: や否や allows a different subject in the second half (he came in and the phone rang). なり requires the same person to act in both halves.
ながら is "while": two actions at the same time (食べながら話す). なり is one action immediately after the other.
が早いか stresses speed; なり stresses that the second action was sudden or unexpected.

mistakes.bad: 彼[かれ]が部屋[へや]に入[はい]る{なり}、電話[でんわ]が鳴[な]った。
mistakes.good: 彼[かれ]が部屋[へや]に入[はい]る{や否[いな]や}、電話[でんわ]が鳴[な]った。
mistakes.note: The phone is a different subject; なり needs the same person in both halves.

mistakes.bad: 私[わたし]は家[いえ]に帰[かえ]る{なり}、シャワーを浴[あ]びた。
mistakes.good: 私[わたし]は家[いえ]に帰[かえ]っ{て}すぐ、シャワーを浴[あ]びた。
mistakes.note: なり describes someone else's striking action as seen by the speaker; for your own routine use てすぐ.

skills.tip: Ask: is it the same person, and would an onlooker say "and then, out of nowhere, he..."? Both yes: なり.

skills.rule: Verb + そばから: "no sooner do I X than it is undone", happening again and again.
skills.explain:
そば is "right beside": the second event follows right on the heels of the first, every time. It describes a repeated pattern, almost always a frustrating one: you tidy and the children mess it up, you learn words and forget them, money comes in and goes straight out.

It takes the dictionary form or the た-form (覚えるそばから, 注意したそばから). The second half is usually non-past, ～ている or ～てしまう, because it states a habit, not a single event.

That is the line to remember: for one event that happened once, use たとたん or や否や. そばから is wrong for a single moment such as "the moment I reached the station, it started raining".

It is written or fairly formal, and carries a tone of complaint or resignation.
patterns: [dictionary-form / た-form verb] そばから、[repeated result, often ～てしまう / ～ている]

examples.jp: 部屋[へや]を片付[かたづ]ける{そばから}、子供[こども]が散[ち]らかす。
examples.en: No sooner do I tidy the room than the kids mess it up again.

examples.jp: 単語[たんご]を覚[おぼ]える{そばから}忘[わす]れてしまう。
examples.en: I forget words as fast as I learn them.

examples.jp: 給料[きゅうりょう]が入[はい]る{そばから}、使[つか]ってしまう。
examples.en: My pay goes out as soon as it comes in.

examples.jp: 雪[ゆき]かきをする{そばから}、また雪[ゆき]が積[つ]もっていく。
examples.en: As fast as I clear the snow, it piles up again.

examples.jp: 弟[おとうと]は注意[ちゅうい]された{そばから}、また同[おな]じいたずらをしている。
examples.en: My little brother gets told off and goes straight back to the same mischief.

contrast.note: たとたん(に) is one event, once, in the past (ドアを開けたとたん、犬が吠えた). そばから is a repeated cycle.
や否や also narrates a single past moment. If the sentence means "every time", it is そばから.
が早いか is one quick reaction. そばから is an effort undone over and over.

mistakes.bad: 駅[えき]に着[つ]いた{そばから}、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]り出[だ]した。
mistakes.good: 駅[えき]に着[つ]いた{とたん}、雨[あめ]が降[ふ]り出[だ]した。
mistakes.note: This happened once; そばから is only for something that keeps recurring.

skills.tip: Can you add "every single time" and "it all gets undone"? Then そばから.
